techniques.name: Membership Inference Attack Testing
techniques.description: Membership inference attack testing evaluates whether adversaries can determine if specific data points were included in a model's training set. This technique simulates attacks where adversaries use model confidence scores, prediction patterns, or loss values to distinguish training data from non-training data. Testing measures privacy leakage by calculating attack success rates, precision-recall trade-offs, and advantage over random guessing. Results inform decisions about privacy-enhancing techniques like differential privacy or regularisation.

example_use_cases.description: Testing a genomics research model to ensure attackers cannot determine which individuals' genetic data were used in training, protecting highly sensitive hereditary and health information from privacy breaches.
Evaluating whether a facial recognition system leaks information about whose faces were in the training set, preventing unauthorized identification of individuals in training data.

Auditing a credit scoring model used by multiple lenders to verify and transparently document that the model doesn't leak information about which specific customers' financial histories were used in training, supporting fair lending compliance reporting.

limitations.description: Attack success rates vary significantly depending on model architecture, training procedures, and data characteristics, making it difficult to establish universal thresholds for acceptable privacy.
Sophisticated attackers with shadow models or auxiliary data may achieve attack success rates 2-3x higher than standard evaluation scenarios test.
Trade-off between model utility and privacy protection means defending against membership inference often reduces model accuracy.
Testing requires access to both training and non-training data from the same distribution, which may not always be available for realistic evaluation.

resources.title: SoK: Membership Inference Attacks on LLMs are Rushing Nowhere (and How to Fix It)
resources.abstract: Whether Large Language models (LLMs) memorize their training data and what this means, from measuring privacy leakage to detecting copyright violations, has become a rapidly growing area of research. In the last few months, more than 10 new methods have been proposed to perform Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) against LLMs. Contrary to traditional MIAs which rely on fixed-but randomized-records or models, these methods are mostly trained and tested on datasets collected post-hoc. Sets of members and non-members, used to evaluate the MIA, are constructed using informed guesses after the release of a model. This lack of randomization raises concerns of a distribution shift between members and non-members. In this work, we first extensively review the literature on MIAs against LLMs and show that, while most work focuses on sequence-level MIAs evaluated in post-hoc setups, a range of target models, motivations and units of interest are considered. We then quantify distribution shifts present in 6 datasets used in the literature, ranging from books to papers using a model-less bag of word classifier and compare the model-less results to the MIA. Our analysis shows that all of these datasets constructed post-hoc suffer from strong distribution shifts. These shifts invalidate the claims of LLMs memorizing strongly in real-world scenarios and, potentially, also the methodological contributions of the recent papers based on these datasets. Yet, all hope might not be lost. In the second part of this work, we introduce important considerations to properly evaluate MIAs against LLMs and discuss, in turn, potential ways forwards: randomized test splits, injections of randomized (unique) sequences, randomized finetuning, and several post-hoc control methods. While each option comes with its advantages and limitations, we believe they collectively provide solid grounds to guide the development of MIA methods and study LLM memorization. We conclude with an overview of recommended approaches to benchmark sequence-level and document-level MIAs against LLMs.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models
resources.abstract: We quantitatively investigate how machine learning models leak information about the individual data records on which they were trained. We focus on the basic membership inference attack: given a data record and black-box access to a model, determine if the record was in the model's training dataset. To perform membership inference against a target model, we make adversarial use of machine learning and train our own inference model to recognize differences in the target model's predictions on the inputs that it trained on versus the inputs that it did not train on. We empirically evaluate our inference techniques on classification models trained by commercial "machine learning as a service" providers such as Google and Amazon. Using realistic datasets and classification tasks, including a hospital discharge dataset whose membership is sensitive from the privacy perspective, we show that these models can be vulnerable to membership inference attacks. We then investigate the factors that influence this leakage and evaluate mitigation strategies.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
resources.abstract: A membership inference attack allows an adversary to query a trained machine learning model to predict whether or not a particular example was contained in the model’s training dataset. These attacks are currently evaluated using average-case “accuracy” metrics that fail to characterize whether the attack can confidently identify any members of the training set. We argue that attacks should instead be evaluated by computing their true-positive rate at low (e.g., ≤ 0.1%) false-positive rates, and find most prior attacks perform poorly when evaluated in this way. To address this we develop a Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) that carefully combines multiple ideas from the literature. Our attack is 10× more powerful at low false-positive rates, and also strictly dominates prior attacks on existing metrics.

resources.title: Assess privacy risks with the TensorFlow Privacy Report
Privacy Risks from Genomic Data-Sharing Beacons
resources.abstract: The human genetics community needs robust protocols that enable secure sharing of genomic data from participants in genetic research. Beacons are web servers that answer allele-presence queries--such as "Do you have a genome that has a specific nucleotide (e.g., A) at a specific genomic position (e.g., position 11,272 on chromosome 1)?"--with either "yes" or "no." Here, we show that individuals in a beacon are susceptible to re-identification even if the only data shared include presence or absence information about alleles in a beacon. Specifically, we propose a likelihood-ratio test of whether a given individual is present in a given genetic beacon. Our test is not dependent on allele frequencies and is the most powerful test for a specified false-positive rate. Through simulations, we showed that in a beacon with 1,000 individuals, re-identification is possible with just 5,000 queries. Relatives can also be identified in the beacon. Re-identification is possible even in the presence of sequencing errors and variant-calling differences. In a beacon constructed with 65 European individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project, we demonstrated that it is possible to detect membership in the beacon with just 250 SNPs. With just 1,000 SNP queries, we were able to detect the presence of an individual genome from the Personal Genome Project in an existing beacon. Our results show that beacons can disclose membership and implied phenotypic information about participants and do not protect privacy a priori. We discuss risk mitigation through policies and standards such as not allowing anonymous pings of genetic beacons and requiring minimum beacon sizes.

sample_claims.text: The genomics research model does not reveal which individuals' genetic data were included in its training dataset
The facial recognition system resists attempts to identify whose images were used during model development
The credit scoring model's documented privacy characteristics include quantified risk of exposing individual customers' training data participation
The medical diagnosis system protects patient privacy by preventing determination of which clinical records were used in training
The recommendation system maintains user privacy even when adversaries systematically probe for training data membership

techniques.name: Synthetic Data Evaluation
techniques.description: Synthetic data evaluation checks whether an artificial dataset made to stand in for sensitive real records is safe to share and still useful, and reports the trade-off between the two. Privacy is tested by simulating an attacker who holds the synthetic data and some facts about a person, and measuring how accurately the attacker can use the data to infer that person's sensitive values. Fidelity is tested by comparing the synthetic and real data column by column and in pairs of columns. Another check trains a classifier to tell the two apart, and a classifier that cannot beat chance suggests they are statistically alike. Utility is tested by running the analyses or training the models the data is meant for on the synthetic data and comparing the results with those from the real data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research office wants to share synthetic outpatient records with university partners. Before release it simulates an attacker who knows each patient's age band, sex and postcode district and tries to infer their diagnosis from the synthetic table, and it withholds the data if the attack does better than guessing from overall diagnosis rates.

A national statistics office gives researchers synthetic microdata for exploratory analysis. After the researchers settle on their models, the office runs the same models on the real data inside a secure environment and compares the estimates, to tell the researchers whether their exploratory conclusions can be trusted.

A bank's fraud team generates synthetic card transactions to share with an external vendor. It compares how often each fraud type appears and how amount, merchant type and time of day relate in the real and synthetic data, then checks that a model trained on the synthetic data still catches rare fraud in held-out real transactions.

limitations.description: Stronger privacy protection usually costs data quality, so the three scores pull against each other. There is no neutral threshold: where to set the balance depends on how sensitive the data is and what it will be used for, and the evaluation reports the trade-off without settling it.

Attack-based privacy tests only probe the attacks and attacker knowledge that were tried. A dataset that resists them may still leak to an attacker with more auxiliary information or a better method, so a good result is not proof of safety.

Fidelity and utility scores depend on which metrics, models and analyses are chosen. A synthetic dataset can match the real data on the columns and column pairs checked yet differ in ways that matter for a particular analysis, and general and analysis-specific utility scores can disagree.

Scores summarise the whole table, so rare events and small subgroups can be lost without moving the totals much. A fraud pattern or a minority group that the generator has smoothed away may show up only if the evaluation is designed to look for it.

The tests need statistical, privacy-engineering and domain expertise to set up and read. A classifier-based fidelity check can be misled by over-fitting or under-fitting the classifier, and weak settings can make poor synthetic data look good.

resources.title: General and Specific Utility Measures for Synthetic Data
resources.abstract: Data holders can produce synthetic versions of data sets when concerns about potential disclosure restrict the availability of the original records. The paper is concerned with methods to judge whether such synthetic data have a distribution that is comparable with that of the original data: what we term general utility. We consider how general utility compares with specific utility: the similarity of results of analyses from the synthetic data and the original data. We adapt a previous general measure of data utility, the propensity score mean-squared error pMSE, to the specific case of synthetic data and derive its distribution for the case when the correct synthesis model is used to create the synthetic data. Our asymptotic results are confirmed by a simulation study. We also consider two specific utility measures, confidence interval overlap and standardized difference in summary statistics, which we compare with the general utility results. We present two contrasting examples of data syntheses: one illustrating synthetic data that is evaluated as being useful by both general and specific measures and the second where neither is the case. For the second case we show how the general utility measures can identify the deficiencies of the synthetic data and suggest how this can inform possible improvements to the synthesis method.

resources.title: Quality Report | SDMetrics
A Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic electronic health record generation models
resources.abstract: Synthetic health data have the potential to mitigate privacy concerns in supporting biomedical research and healthcare applications. Modern approaches for data generation continue to evolve and demonstrate remarkable potential. Yet there is a lack of a systematic assessment framework to benchmark methods as they emerge and determine which methods are most appropriate for which use cases. In this work, we introduce a systematic benchmarking framework to appraise key characteristics with respect to utility and privacy metrics. We apply the framework to evaluate synthetic data generation methods for electronic health records data from two large academic medical centers with respect to several use cases. The results illustrate that there is a utility-privacy tradeoff for sharing synthetic health data and further indicate that no method is unequivocally the best on all criteria in each use case, which makes it evident why synthetic data generation methods need to be assessed in context.

resources.title: Generating and Evaluating Synthetic UK Primary Care Data: Preserving Data Utility & Patient Privacy
resources.abstract: There is increasing interest in the potential of synthetic data to validate and benchmark machine learning algorithms as well as reveal any biases in real-world data used for algorithm development. This paper discusses the key requirements of synthetic data for such purposes and proposes an approach to generating and evaluating synthetic data that meets these requirements. We propose a framework to generate and evaluate synthetic data with the aim of simultaneously preserving the complexities of ground truth data in the synthetic data whilst also ensuring privacy. We include as a case study, a proof-of-concept synthetic dataset modelled on UK primary care data to demonstrate the application of this framework.

sample_claims.text: In the attack tests run on this release, an attacker who holds the synthetic patient dataset and a person's demographic details infers that person's diagnosis no more accurately, within a stated margin, than from population rates alone
Estimates from the researchers' models fitted to the synthetic microdata agree with the same models fitted to the real data within the stated tolerance
The fraud model trained on synthetic transactions performs within the stated tolerance of the real-data-trained comparison model on the same independent real-data test set
The synthetic dataset meets the stated agreement targets for the selected environmental analyses compared with the real reference data

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Differential Privacy Auditing
techniques.description: Differential privacy auditing tests whether a training procedure that claims a differential privacy guarantee at a stated budget (epsilon, where smaller means stronger privacy) loses more privacy in practice than the claim allows, by measuring a statistical lower bound on its true epsilon. The guarantee itself comes from a mathematical proof, and membership inference testing reports attack success on real records for any model; the audit instead controls which records are present and asks whether the code that was run honours the proof, so it can expose an implementation bug or accounting error but can never confirm the guarantee. The auditor builds two training sets that differ only by one or a few planted records, called canaries and often crafted to be easy to detect, trains the model many times on each, and applies a fixed test to every trained model to guess whether the canary was present. Confidence intervals for the test's true-positive and false-positive rates, such as Clopper-Pearson intervals for a proportion, are converted into a value of epsilon that the procedure must exceed at a stated confidence level, such as 99 per cent; a bound above the claimed epsilon shows that the claim is false for that implementation. Because hundreds of training runs are costly, a later design needs only one: many canaries are each included or left out at random, the test guesses which were included, and the share of correct guesses gives the bound, which is looser than the many-run design's.

example_use_cases.description: Before an NHS trust releases a readmission-risk model trained with an open-source differential privacy library at a claimed epsilon of 3, its data science team audits the exact code and settings: it trains several hundred models with and without a planted mislabelled record and signs off only if the 99 per cent lower bound stays below 3, recording that the audit could have caught a violation but cannot prove the guarantee.

The maintainers of a differentially private training library run a white-box audit on every release: the auditor sees each intermediate model update and inserts a gradient crafted to be easy to detect, so a change to the clipping or noise-sampling code that silently weakens the guarantee pushes the lower bound above the budget the library reports and fails the build.

A mobile keyboard team training a next-word model with federated learning under a claimed user-level guarantee adds simulated canary users to its single production training run, each included or left out at random and enough of them that a bound above the claim is reachable, and checks the one-run lower bound against the claim, because retraining the federated model hundreds of times is not feasible.

limitations.description: A result below the claim proves nothing. The bound is only as strong as the audit behind it: weak canaries, a test that sees only the final model, or too few runs or canaries can give bounds far below the claimed epsilon (one library's documented single-run audit with 1,000 canaries reported 0.42 for a model trained at epsilon 68.5, and 5.5 for one trained without differential privacy). Only a bound above the claim is conclusive, and a pass must not be reported as confirming the guarantee.

The number of training runs caps what can be detected. With 500 runs per training set and 99 per cent confidence, the largest bound the original method can report is about 4.5 even if the test never errs, so it cannot show a claimed epsilon of 8 to be false; larger budgets need many more runs or a different design. In the single-run design the number of canaries sets the cap in the same way.

Bounds come close to the claim only under the strongest access. For DP-SGD on natural data, audits match the claimed epsilon when the auditor sees every intermediate update and inserts crafted gradients, the setting the standard proof assumes. With crafted input records, seeing every update helps only slightly over the final model, and with the final model most of the original audit's bounds were roughly 7 to 12 times below the claim. A result holds only for the access and canaries it assumed.

It is expensive. The original method trained 500 models per training set to choose the test's threshold and another 500 per set to estimate its error rates, which is impractical for large models. The single-run design avoids this but gives looser bounds, which weaken further when only the final model is seen and the model cannot memorise all the canaries or other training data is added.

It checks one implementation, configuration and pair of datasets. A change of clipping norm, batch size, random initialisation or library version needs a new audit, and canaries that are typical rather than worst-case can miss a violation that affects only unusual records, giving false confidence about the risk to outliers.

resources.title: Auditing Differentially Private Machine Learning: How Private is Private SGD?
resources.abstract: We investigate whether Differentially Private SGD offers better privacy in practice than what is guaranteed by its state-of-the-art analysis. We do so via novel data poisoning attacks, which we show correspond to realistic privacy attacks. While previous work (Ma et al., arXiv 2019) proposed this connection between differential privacy and data poisoning as a defense against data poisoning, our use as a tool for understanding the privacy of a specific mechanism is new. More generally, our work takes a quantitative, empirical approach to understanding the privacy afforded by specific implementations of differentially private algorithms that we believe has the potential to complement and influence analytical work on differential privacy.

techniques.name: Training Data Extraction Testing
techniques.description: Training data extraction testing measures how much of its training text a generative language model reproduces word for word when it is sampled, without the tester supplying any training record to look for. It differs from membership inference testing, which starts from a candidate record and asks only whether that record was used in training, and from canary exposure testing, which needs secrets planted before training. The tester prompts the model with empty prompts or a few words taken from public text, generates a large volume of output (from tens of millions to billions of tokens) with the sampling settings the deployed system uses, and checks it against the training corpus: any span of at least a fixed length, such as 50 tokens, found verbatim in an index of the corpus, and not low-entropy filler such as repeated characters or lists of numbers, counts as extracted, and personal data is checked by tagging names and identifiers in the output and looking them up in the corpus. Where the corpus cannot be searched, the outputs are ranked by how much more probable the model finds them than a smaller reference model or a text-compression algorithm does, and the top-ranked candidates are checked by hand, for example by web search. The result is the share of generated text copied from training data (under the hand-checked route, the number confirmed among the candidates checked), the number of distinct passages extracted, and the passages themselves, each with a count of the training documents that contain it: a passage found in one or two documents is a privacy finding in a way that a licence or news story repeated thousands of times is not.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's privacy engineering team fine-tunes an open-weight language model on ten years of customer-service chat transcripts to draft replies for agents. Before deployment it generates 50 million tokens from public-text prompts with the production sampling settings, searches an index of the transcripts for 50-token matches, and looks up every account number, name and phone number tagged in the output. It runs the same test on the base model as a control.

A hospital research group that trained a clinical note-completion model on de-identified discharge summaries runs the test before sharing the weights with partner hospitals. Besides searching for verbatim passages of the summaries, it tags patient names, dates of birth and NHS numbers in the generated text and looks each up in the training set, to find identifiers the de-identification step missed and decide whether the summaries must be re-scrubbed and the model retrained.

An AI developer preparing an open-weight release compares two checkpoints, one trained on a deduplicated copy of the pre-training corpus. It generates text from each at budgets of 100 million and 1 billion tokens, counts distinct 50-token passages found verbatim in the corpus, and compares how the counts grow with the budget, not a single rate, before choosing which checkpoint to release and what to say about memorisation in the model card.

A government department running a citizen-facing chat assistant on a model it fine-tuned on casework correspondence repeats the test after every fine-tuning update. Because chat-tuned models can leak little under ordinary prompts yet emit training text once pushed off their chat behaviour, the test also uses prompts asking the assistant to repeat a single word many times, a pattern that made one production assistant reproduce its training data.

limitations.description: The result is a lower bound set by the effort spent. The number of distinct passages extracted keeps growing as more text is generated, and one study found that a model which leaked more than another at a small budget leaked less in total. A clean result, or a comparison of models at one fixed budget, can therefore mislead; report the generation budget and compare models at several budgets.

Much memorised text comes out only after the right prompt. In one study, sampling from short public prompts recovered about a third of the passages a model was known to reproduce when given their true opening words, and a chat-tuned model leaked far less under ordinary prompts than when pushed into repeating a word. A low rate under ordinary prompts is weak evidence that the data cannot be extracted.

The verdict depends on what the output is checked against and on the match rule. A public proxy for an unavailable corpus undercounts (in one study a 9 TB proxy found under half the matches a manual web search found), and a minimum match length long enough to rule out coincidence misses short secrets such as phone or account numbers unless they are tagged and looked up separately. Paraphrased leaks and facts stitched together from several documents are not counted.

It is costly at a useful scale. One study generated a billion tokens per model, and its whole evaluation, including a 45 TB index built over a 9 TB corpus, took three weeks on a large cloud machine. The test also produces copies of any personal data the model leaks, which must be stored, reviewed and deleted under the same controls as the training data.

It shows what the model emits, not what an attacker could infer. It does not say whether a known person's record was used in training, and it gives no bound for data the test did not happen to elicit, so a clean result cannot stand in for a formal guarantee such as differential privacy.

techniques.name: Attacker-Model Re-identification Risk Measurement
techniques.description: Attacker-model re-identification risk measurement estimates, for a table of real records about people that is about to be released or shared, the probability that an attacker who links it with other information could correctly match a record to the person it describes. This record follows the attacker models of El Emam and Dankar (prosecutor and journalist) and of Dankar and El Emam (marketer), as implemented in the ARX tool: the assessor lists the quasi-identifiers (columns such as age, sex, postcode and admission date that an attacker could know or find), groups the records that share the same values on them, and names the attacker being guarded against. For a prosecutor, who knows the target is in the table, a record's risk is one over the size of its group in the table; for a journalist, who does not know this and links to a register of the wider population, it is one over the size of the matching group in that population, estimated with a statistical model when the population counts are not known; for a marketer, who tries to match as many records as possible, the measure is the expected share of records matched correctly. The assessor reports the highest record risk, the average risk and the share of records above a threshold set for the release, which decides whether the table can go out as it is or needs more generalisation or suppression first. It measures how easily records can be matched to people under the stated assumptions, unlike k-anonymity, which transforms the data, and it does not measure what can be learned about someone from values their whole group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A health insurer releasing claims data for a public prediction competition assumes an attacker who knows a neighbour's age, sex and a few of their claims, and measures each record's risk as one over the size of its group among all the insurer's members. It generalises ages and procedure codes until the measured probability of re-identification is below the 0.05 threshold agreed for the release, then checks the result with simulated matching attacks.

A pharmaceutical company sharing participant-level data from a completed trial with external researchers measures risk against the wider population, not the trial sample, because the participants are a small sample of everyone with the condition. It estimates how many records are unique in that population with ARX's uniqueness models and records the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, estimator and threshold in the data-sharing agreement for the researchers' data access committee to review.

A city transport authority planning to give a commuting dataset of home district, work district, age band and usual travel times to a contractor training a demand-forecasting model runs the assessment, finds a large share of records unique on home and work district together, merges small districts before sharing, and re-runs the assessment to confirm that the share of records above its threshold has fallen below the agreed limit.

limitations.description: The numbers are only as good as the list of quasi-identifiers and the attacker model behind them. A column left off the list, or an attacker who knows more (several of a person's hospital visits rather than one), can make records far easier to match than the assessment reports, and the assessor has to guess what other data an attacker holds. Repeating the assessment for stronger attackers, as some releases do with simulated matching, shows how sensitive the result is to these guesses.

It measures the chance of finding which record is a person's, not what can be learned about them. If all 20 records in a group share the same diagnosis, each has a measured risk of 1 in 20, yet anyone known to belong to the group has their diagnosis disclosed. Checks on the sensitive values, such as l-diversity, are needed alongside it when the release contains sensitive columns.

The journalist measure needs to know how common each record's values are in the wider population, which is rarely known and is estimated from the sample with statistical models; an evaluation of four estimators of population uniqueness on six clinical datasets found none accurate in all conditions. A small sample does not make re-identification unlikely in itself: one study estimated that 15 demographic attributes would let 99.98 per cent of Americans be correctly re-identified in any dataset.

There is no universal threshold, and the measure chosen changes the answer. For the same records the prosecutor measure is always at least as high as the journalist measure, so applying it to a release that is a small sample of a population over-protects and strips detail the data's users need; El Emam and Dankar found this effect strongest at small sampling fractions. The threshold, and which measure it applies to, must be justified for each release.

It measures one table as released, at one time. An attacker can combine several releases of the same data, or successive versions of a table that is updated, and longitudinal data, where each person has many events, need the attacker's knowledge of several events to be modelled explicitly. The basic measures do neither, so each additional or updated release needs its own assessment that takes the earlier ones into account.

sample_claims.text: Under a prosecutor attack using age band, sex and postcode district, no record in the released extract has a re-identification probability above 0.09.
The expected proportion of records in the competition dataset that an attacker could correctly match by linking it to the state voter register is below 0.1 per cent.

The re-identification risk assessment for the shared trial data states the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, population estimator and threshold used, and the highest record risk is below the agreed threshold.
Fewer than 1 per cent of records in the commuting dataset shared with the contractor are estimated to be unique in the city's population on home district, work district and age band.
